#10727. Web Performance Optimization: Practical Techniques for Building Faster Websites

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Website performance is an essential part of modern web development. A visually attractive website may still frustrate users if its pages load slowly, interactions feel delayed, or content shifts unexpectedly during loading. These problems can affect usability, accessibility, and business outcomes.

Improving performance does not always require a complete redesign or a complicated optimization framework. Many improvements come from understanding how browsers load resources, reducing unnecessary work, optimizing images, and delivering only the code a page actually needs.

For developers, the challenge is to identify which changes will make the biggest difference without introducing unnecessary complexity.

This article explores practical techniques for improving website performance using modern HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and browser development tools.

The first step in performance optimization is understanding how a website behaves under real conditions.

A page may feel fast on a powerful development computer but perform poorly on a mobile device or a slower network. Measuring performance helps developers identify the actual source of the problem instead of making changes based on assumptions.

Three important Core Web Vitals help evaluate the user experience:

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): Measures when the largest relevant content element becomes visible.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP): Measures responsiveness across user interactions.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): Measures unexpected visual movement during page loading and use.

Current good-target thresholds are an LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, an INP of 200 milliseconds or less, and a CLS of 0.1 or less, assessed at the 75th percentile of page visits.

Developers can investigate performance using Chrome DevTools, Lighthouse, and PageSpeed Insights.

Lab tests are useful during development, while real-user data can reveal problems that synthetic tests may not capture. Whenever possible, examine both.

Images often account for a significant portion of a webpage's downloaded resources. Large images can delay the appearance of important content, particularly on mobile connections.

Modern image formats such as WebP and AVIF can reduce file sizes compared with many traditional image formats, depending on the image and encoding settings.

HTML also provides responsive image features that let the browser choose an appropriate resource.

The srcset attribute provides multiple image candidates, while sizes describes the expected rendered width under different conditions. The browser can use this information to select a suitable resource.

The width and height attributes also help the browser reserve the correct aspect ratio before the image loads, reducing the risk of layout shifts.

For images below the initial viewport, native lazy loading can avoid downloading resources before they are needed:

Avoid applying lazy loading indiscriminately to the main image that users need to see immediately. Delaying the loading of a prominent hero image can worsen LCP.

The best approach is to compress images appropriately, provide suitable dimensions, and choose loading behavior according to each image's position and importance.

Browsers must process certain resources before they can render a page or display it as intended. Large stylesheets and synchronously loaded JavaScript can delay the initial rendering process.

For a typical application entry point, a module script may be appropriate:

Module scripts are deferred by default, allowing the browser to finish parsing the HTML before executing the module.

For non-module scripts that do not depend on a particular execution order, defer can also be useful:

The defer attribute allows the browser to download the script while parsing HTML and execute it after parsing completes.

However, these approaches are not interchangeable in every situation. Developers should consider script dependencies and whether a resource is essential to the initial experience.

CSS also deserves attention. Removing unused rules, splitting styles when appropriate, and delivering critical styles efficiently can help the browser render important content sooner.

The objective is not to eliminate every resource from the initial page. It is to prioritize the resources required to display useful content and support immediate interactions.

Large JavaScript bundles increase the amount of code that browsers must download, parse, compile, and execute.

If an application loads every feature immediately, users may pay the cost of functionality they never use.

Dynamic imports provide a way to load optional modules when needed:

In this example, the chart module is requested when the user activates the relevant button.

This technique can be useful for dashboards, rich editors, maps, and other features that are not necessary for the initial page.

Bundlers can also split application code by route or feature, allowing separate sections of a website to load different JavaScript chunks.

Nevertheless, excessive code splitting can introduce additional network requests and delay features that users need immediately. Developers should measure the results and avoid making essential interactions wait for unnecessary downloads.

The browser calculates element positions and dimensions when laying out a page. Certain JavaScript patterns can force synchronous layout calculations, especially when code repeatedly alternates between changing styles and reading layout-dependent properties.

Each iteration changes a style and then reads a layout-dependent property. Depending on the browser's pending rendering work, this pattern can cause repeated layout calculations.

This reduces the interleaving of layout changes and measurements.

Another useful technique is to update CSS classes rather than modifying many individual properties:

The corresponding CSS can manage the presentation:

These techniques are not guarantees of faster rendering in every case. Browser behavior depends on the complete rendering pipeline, so developers should profile complex interfaces before and after making changes.

Repeatedly downloading the same resources wastes bandwidth and can make subsequent visits slower.

HTTP caching allows browsers to reuse previously downloaded resources when the server's caching policy permits it.

For versioned static assets, a long-lived cache policy can be appropriate:

This example is suitable only when the resource URL changes whenever its contents change. A filename containing a content hash is one common approach.

For HTML documents that change frequently, a shorter cache lifetime or revalidation strategy may be more appropriate.

Compression can further reduce the amount of data transferred. Servers and hosting platforms commonly support Brotli or gzip for compressible text-based resources, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and JSON.

A sound caching strategy distinguishes between stable static assets and content that needs frequent updates. Incorrect caching rules can cause users to receive outdated files, so cache invalidation must be considered during deployment.

Unexpected movement can make a website difficult to use. A button may move just as someone attempts to click it, or an article heading may shift when an image appears above it.

Images should generally include explicit dimensions or a defined aspect ratio:

For embedded media, reserving the expected space can prevent content from jumping after the external resource loads.

Developers should also be careful when inserting banners, advertisements, and dynamically loaded components above existing content. Reserving appropriate space or inserting content in response to a user action can reduce unexpected movement.

A low CLS score is not achieved simply by eliminating animations. The focus is on preventing unexpected layout changes that disrupt the user experience.

JavaScript that occupies the main thread for too long can delay input handling and rendering.

For example, processing a large dataset inside one uninterrupted loop may prevent the browser from responding promptly to user interactions.

When the work can be divided safely, smaller batches can give the browser opportunities to process other tasks:

This example yields between batches using a timer. It illustrates the general idea, but it is not a universal scheduling solution: timers can be delayed, and the appropriate batch size depends on the workload.

For CPU-intensive calculations, Web Workers may be more suitable because they can move supported computation away from the main thread.

Developers should first determine whether the delay comes from JavaScript execution, rendering, network activity, or another source. The right optimization depends on the cause.

Performance optimization works best as an ongoing engineering practice rather than a one-time cleanup.

A repeatable process might include the following steps:

Record a baseline using representative devices and network conditions.

Identify the slowest important operation or resource.

Repeat the measurements under comparable conditions.

Test functionality, accessibility, and visual behavior.

Monitor real-user performance after deployment.

Automated performance checks can help detect regressions during development. However, a single Lighthouse score should not be treated as a complete representation of user experience because results can vary with test conditions.

For websites with significant traffic, field data can reveal differences between devices, geographic regions, and page types.

The most useful optimization is one that produces a measurable improvement without introducing maintenance problems or degrading functionality.

Building a faster website requires a combination of careful measurement and practical engineering decisions. Responsive images, efficient script loading, appropriate caching, reduced layout work, and better task scheduling can all contribute to a smoother user experience.

The key is to prioritize improvements according to their actual impact. Reducing a large image may be more valuable than rewriting a small function, while splitting a JavaScript bundle may help only if the initial page does not need all of its code.

By using browser performance tools, testing realistic scenarios, and monitoring results after deployment, developers can build websites that are more responsive, efficient, and maintainable.

#10726. AI reads brain MRIs in seconds and flags emergencies

A newly developed artificial intelligence system from the University of Michigan can analyze brain MRI scans and deliver a diagnosis in a matter of seconds, according to a new study. The model identified neurological conditions with accuracy reaching 97.5% and was also able to assess how urgently patients needed medical care.

Researchers say this first-of-its-kind technology has the potential to reshape how brain imaging is handled across health systems in the United States. The findings were published in Nature Biomedical Engineering.

"As the global demand for MRI rises and places significant strain our physicians and health systems, our AI model has potential to reduce burden by improving diagnosis and treatment with fast, accurate information," said senior author Todd Hollon, M.D., a neurosurgeon at University of Michigan Health and assistant professor of neurosurgery at U-M Medical School.

Hollon named the new technology Prima. Over a one-year period, his research team evaluated the system using more than 30,000 MRI studies.

Across more than 50 different radiologic diagnoses involving major neurological disorders, Prima delivered stronger diagnostic performance than other advanced AI models. In addition to identifying disease, the system also proved capable of determining which cases required higher priority.

Certain neurological conditions, including strokes and brain hemorrhages, demand immediate medical attention. Hollon said that in these situations, Prima can automatically alert health care providers so action can be taken quickly.

The system was designed to notify the most appropriate subspecialist, such as a stroke neurologist or neurosurgeon. Feedback becomes available immediately after a patient completes imaging.

"Accuracy is paramount when reading a brain MRI, but quick turnaround times are critical for timely diagnosis and improved outcomes," said Yiwei Lyu, M.S., co-first author and postdoctoral fellow of Computer Science and Engineering at U-M.

"At key steps in the process, our results show how Prima can improve workflows and streamline clinical care without abandoning accuracy."

Prima is classified as a vision language model (VLM), a type of artificial intelligence that can process images, video, and text together in real time. While artificial intelligence has been applied to MRI analysis before, researchers say Prima takes a different approach.

Earlier models were typically trained on carefully selected subsets of MRI data and designed to perform narrow tasks, such as identifying lesions or estimating dementia risk. Prima was trained on a much broader dataset.

Hollon's team used every available MRI collected since radiology records were digitized at University of Michigan Health. This included more than 200,000 MRI studies and 5.6 million imaging sequences. The model also incorporated patients' clinical histories and the reasons physicians ordered each imaging study.

"Prima works like a radiologist by integrating information regarding the patient's medical history and imaging data to produce a comprehensive understanding of their health," said co-first author Samir Harake, a data scientist in Hollon's Machine Learning in Neurosurgery Lab.

"This enables better performance across a broad range of prediction tasks."

Addressing MRI Delays and Radiology Shortages

Each year, millions of MRI scans are performed worldwide, many of them focused on neurological disease. Researchers say the demand for these scans is growing faster than the availability of neuroradiology services.

This imbalance has contributed to staffing shortages, diagnostic delays, and errors. Depending on where a patient receives a scan, results may take days or even longer to return.

"Whether you are receiving a scan at a larger health system that is facing increasing volume or a rural hospital with limited resources, innovative technologies are needed to improve access to radiology services," said Vikas Gulani, M.D. Ph.D., co-author and chair of the Department of Radiology at U-M Health.

"Our teams at University of Michigan have collaborated to develop a cutting-edge solution to this problem with tremendous, scalable potential."

Although Prima performed strongly, researchers emphasize that the work is still in an early evaluation phase. Future research will focus on incorporating more detailed patient information and electronic medical record data to further improve diagnostic accuracy.

This approach mirrors how radiologists and physicians interpret MRIs and other imaging studies in real clinical settings. While artificial intelligence is already used in health care, most existing systems are limited to narrowly defined tasks.

Hollon describes Prima as "ChatGPT for medical imaging," noting that similar technology could eventually be adapted for other imaging types, including mammograms, chest X-rays and ultrasounds.

"Like the way AI tools can help draft an email or provide recommendations, Prima aims to be a co-pilot for interpreting medical imaging studies," Hollon said.

"We believe that Prima exemplifies the transformative potential of integrating health systems and AI-driven models to improve health care through innovation."

Additional authors: Asadur Chowdury, M.S., Soumyanil Banerjee, M.S., Rachel Gologorsky, Shixuan Liu, Anna-Katharina Meissner, M.D., Akshay Rao, Chenhui Zhao, Akhil Kondepudi, Cheng Jiang, Xinhai Hou, Rushikesh S. Joshi, M.D., Volker Neuschmelting, M.D., Ashok Srinivasan, M.D., Dawn Kleindorfer, M.D., Brian Athey, Ph.D., Aditya Pandey, M.D., and Honglak Lee, Ph.D., all of University of Michigan.

The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the NIH.

#10722. Brain inspired machines are better at math than expected

Computers designed to mimic the structure of the human brain are showing an unexpected strength. They can solve some of the demanding mathematical equations that lie at the heart of major scientific and engineering problems.

In a study published in Nature Machine Intelligence, Sandia National Laboratories computational neuroscientists Brad Theilman and Brad Aimone introduced a new algorithm that allows neuromorphic hardware to solve partial differential equations, or PDEs -- the mathematical foundation for modeling phenomena such as fluid dynamics, electromagnetic fields and structural mechanics.

The results demonstrate that neuromorphic systems can handle these equations efficiently. The advance could help open the door to the first neuromorphic supercomputer, offering a new path toward energy efficient computing for national security and other critical applications.

The research was funded by the Department of Energy's Office of Science through the Advanced Scientific Computing Research and Basic Energy Sciences programs, as well as the National Nuclear Security Administration's Advanced Simulation and Computing program.

Solving Partial Differential Equations With Brain Like Hardware

Partial differential equations are essential for simulating real world systems. They are used to forecast weather, analyze how materials respond to stress, and model complex physical processes. Traditionally, solving PDEs requires enormous computing power. Neuromorphic computers approach the problem differently by processing information in ways that resemble how the brain operates.

"We're just starting to have computational systems that can exhibit intelligent-like behavior. But they look nothing like the brain, and the amount of resources that they require is ridiculous, frankly," Theilman said.

For years, neuromorphic systems were mainly viewed as tools for pattern recognition or for speeding up artificial neural networks. Few expected them to manage mathematically rigorous problems such as PDEs, which are typically handled by large scale supercomputers.

Aimone and Theilman were not surprised by the outcome. They argue that the human brain routinely carries out highly complex calculations, even if people are unaware of it.

"Pick any sort of motor control task -- like hitting a tennis ball or swinging a bat at a baseball," Aimone said. "These are very sophisticated computations. They are exascale-level problems that our brains are capable of doing very cheaply."

Energy Efficient Computing for National Security

The findings could have major implications for the National Nuclear Security Administration, which is responsible for maintaining the nation's nuclear deterrent. Supercomputers used across the nuclear weapons complex consume vast amounts of electricity to simulate the physics of nuclear systems and other high stakes scenarios.

Neuromorphic computing may provide a way to significantly cut energy use while still delivering strong computational performance. By solving PDEs in a brain inspired manner, these systems suggest that large simulations could be run using far less power than conventional supercomputers require.

"You can solve real physics problems with brain-like computation," Aimone said. "That's something you wouldn't expect because people's intuition goes the opposite way. And in fact, that intuition is often wrong."

The team envisions neuromorphic supercomputers eventually becoming central to Sandia's mission of protecting national security.

What Neuromorphic Computing Reveals About the Brain

Beyond engineering advances, the research also touches on deeper questions about intelligence and how the brain performs calculations. The algorithm developed by Theilman and Aimone closely mirrors the structure and behavior of cortical networks.

"We based our circuit on a relatively well-known model in the computational neuroscience world," Theilman said. "We've shown the model has a natural but non-obvious link to PDEs, and that link hasn't been made until now -- 12 years after the model was introduced."

The researchers believe this work could help connect neuroscience with applied mathematics, offering new understanding of how the brain processes information.

"Diseases of the brain could be diseases of computation," Aimone said. "But we don't have a solid grasp on how the brain performs computations yet."

If that idea proves correct, neuromorphic computing might one day contribute to better understanding and treatment of neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

Building the Next Generation of Supercomputers

Neuromorphic computing remains an emerging field, but this work represents an important step forward. The Sandia team hopes their results will encourage collaboration among mathematicians, neuroscientists and engineers to expand what this technology can achieve.

"If we've already shown that we can import this relatively basic but fundamental applied math algorithm into neuromorphic -- is there a corresponding neuromorphic formulation for even more advanced applied math techniques?" Theilman said.

As development continues, the researchers are optimistic. "We have a foot in the door for understanding the scientific questions, but also we have something that solves a real problem," Theilman said.

#10720. Designing Maintainable CSS Architecture: A Practical Guide to Scalable Stylesheets

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

CSS is easy to write when a website contains only a handful of components. As an application grows, however, stylesheets can become difficult to manage. A change intended for one button may affect several unrelated components; repeated declarations accumulate, and developers begin adding increasingly specific selectors to override earlier rules.

These problems are rarely caused by CSS itself. They often result from unclear styling conventions, poorly defined component boundaries, and a lack of consistent decisions about how styles should be organized.

A maintainable CSS architecture provides a predictable structure for writing, extending, and debugging styles. It does not require a particular framework or a complicated build process. Instead, it relies on clear naming, controlled scope, reusable design tokens, and an understanding of the CSS cascade.

This guide explores practical techniques for creating CSS that remains understandable as a website grows.

A CSS architecture defines how developers organize styles and how different parts of a stylesheet interact.

Without shared conventions, one developer might use deeply nested selectors, another might rely on element IDs, and a third might repeatedly override existing rules. Each approach may work in isolation, but the combined stylesheet becomes harder to reason about.

These selectors repeat the same styling intent while depending on different structural paths. Changes to the HTML can also break the relationship between the selector and its target.

A simpler approach is to give the component a meaningful class:

The shorter selector communicates the styling intent directly and is easier to reuse.

The objective is not to make every selector as short as possible. It is to ensure that selectors express a clear relationship between a component and its presentation.

A growing interface often uses the same colors, spacing values, border radii, and typography rules across multiple components.

Repeating these values throughout a stylesheet makes future changes unnecessarily difficult. CSS custom properties provide a central place for shared design decisions.

If the primary brand color changes, developers can update the token instead of searching through multiple component rules.

Tokens are also useful for implementing themes:

This example changes selected design values for a dark theme. A complete theme should also consider text contrast, interactive states, shadows, and other visual properties rather than changing only three variables.

For smaller websites, a few custom properties may be enough. Larger design systems may benefit from clearly defined token categories for colors, typography, spacing, and component-specific values.

CSS class names should help developers understand which component a rule belongs to and what the rule represents.

One established approach is BEM, which stands for Block, Element, Modifier.

The corresponding classes communicate different roles:

article-card__title identifies an element within that component.

article-card__link--featured Represents a variation of the link.

This convention can make class names more predictable, especially when several developers work on the same project.

However, BEM is a naming convention, not a requirement. Other approaches can work equally well when they are applied consistently. The important consideration is that class names remain understandable and do not depend excessively on the component's current position in the document.

CSS specificity determines how competing selectors are prioritized, alongside factors such as origin, importance, cascade layers, and source order.

Problems arise when developers repeatedly increase specificity to override earlier rules.

The second selector is more specific, which makes later changes harder to manage.

A more maintainable approach is to keep component rules focused:

A modifier class now expresses the intended variation explicitly.

For larger projects, cascade layers can establish a predictable order between groups of styles:

This example declares the intended order of the layers. Normal declarations in later layers take precedence over competing normal declarations in earlier layers, subject to the CSS cascade rules.

Cascade layers can reduce the need for increasingly specific selectors, but developers should understand how layered and unlayered styles interact before introducing them into an existing project.

A maintainable stylesheet structure should help developers find the relevant rules without searching through an enormous file.

For example, a component-oriented project might use this organization:

reset.css normalizes selected browser defaults.

layout.css manages larger page structures.

components/ contains component-specific rules.

utilities.css provides small, reusable helper classes.

This structure is an example rather than a universal template. A small static website may be easier to maintain with one or two stylesheets, while a larger application may benefit from a modular system.

The decision should reflect the project's complexity, team size, build tooling, and expected lifespan.

Splitting CSS into many files without clear responsibilities can create more overhead rather than less.

Responsive styling becomes difficult to maintain when media queries are scattered throughout the codebase without a consistent strategy.

Developers can simplify responsive rules by using flexible layout primitives where possible and reserving media queries for meaningful changes in presentation.

This layout automatically adjusts the number of columns according to the available space.

For typography, a fluid value can reduce the need for multiple font-size breakpoints:

The clamp() function keeps the font size between a minimum and a maximum while allowing it to scale fluidly in between.

These techniques do not eliminate media queries. Navigation patterns, page composition, and other design decisions may still require explicit breakpoints.

A useful architecture distinguishes between properties that can adapt naturally and changes that require a deliberate layout transition.

Interactive components often have several visual states, including hover, focus, active, disabled, and invalid.

If each state is implemented differently across the application, the interface can become inconsistent.

A shared button component can establish predictable behavior:

This example gives the component a consistent baseline and defines visible focus and disabled states.

Developers should still check contrast and keyboard behavior, and ensure that disabled styling is paired with actual disabled functionality where appropriate.

A reusable component should not merely look consistent. It should also behave predictably across the application.

Reusable CSS can reduce duplication, but creating an abstraction for every repeated declaration can make the code harder to understand.

Suppose two components share only a small amount of spacing. Creating a complicated class hierarchy to reuse those few declarations may not provide meaningful value.

On the other hand, a repeated button pattern used across dozens of pages is a strong candidate for a shared component style.

Does this pattern appear in multiple places?

Does it represent a meaningful design concept?

Would a shared rule make future changes easier?

Can the abstraction be understood without tracing several unrelated stylesheets?

If the answers suggest that reuse will improve clarity, a shared rule or component is likely worthwhile.

Otherwise, a straightforward local declaration may be the better choice.

A stylesheet can become difficult to maintain even when its original architecture is sound. New features, temporary overrides, and inconsistent contributions can gradually undermine the conventions.

Automated tools can help enforce standards. Stylelint, for example, can identify certain syntax problems and enforce configurable style rules.

Consistent formatting and naming conventions.

Visual regression tests for important page layouts.

Browser testing at representative viewport sizes.

Accessibility checks for focus visibility and color contrast.

Unused CSS should be removed carefully. A class that appears unused in a static search may be generated dynamically by JavaScript or applied through a content management system.

Similarly, visual regression tests should be interpreted in context because font rendering and browser differences can produce legitimate variations.

The purpose of these practices is to catch unintended changes before they become difficult-to-diagnose production problems.

Maintainable CSS architecture depends on clarity and consistency, not the number of tools or files a project uses. Design tokens centralize shared values, meaningful class names improve readability, controlled specificity reduces conflicts, and sensible stylesheet organization makes components easier to maintain.

Responsive layout primitives and reusable interaction states further reduce duplication, while automated checks help prevent conventions from deteriorating as a project grows.

The most effective architecture is one that fits the actual needs of the website and its developers. By establishing a small set of clear rules and applying them consistently, teams can create stylesheets that remain flexible, understandable, and easier to extend over time.

#10716. Quantum computer breakthrough tracks qubit fluctuations in real time

Researchers at the Niels Bohr Institute have significantly increased how quickly changes in delicate quantum states can be detected inside a qubit. By combining commercially available hardware with new adaptive measurement techniques, the team can now observe rapid shifts in qubit behavior that were previously impossible to see.

Qubits are the fundamental units of quantum computers, which scientists hope will one day outperform today's most powerful machines. But qubits are extremely sensitive. The materials used to build them often contain tiny defects that scientists still do not fully understand. These microscopic imperfections can shift position hundreds of times per second. As they move, they alter how quickly a qubit loses energy and with it valuable quantum information.

Until recently, standard testing methods took up to a minute to measure qubit performance. That was far too slow to capture these rapid fluctuations. Instead, researchers could only determine an average energy loss rate, masking the true and often unstable behavior of the qubit.

It is somewhat like asking a strong workhorse to pull a plow while obstacles constantly appear in its path faster than anyone can react. The animal may be capable, but unpredictable disruptions make the job much harder.

A research team from the Niels Bohr Institute's Center for Quantum Devices and the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme, led by postdoctoral researcher Dr. Fabrizio Berritta, developed a real time adaptive measurement system that tracks changes in the qubit energy loss (relaxation) rate as they occur. The project involved collaboration with scientists from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Leiden University, and Chalmers University.

The new approach relies on a fast classical controller that updates its estimate of a qubit's relaxation rate within milliseconds. This matches the natural speed of the fluctuations themselves, rather than lagging seconds or minutes behind as older methods did.

To achieve this, the team used a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), a type of classical processor designed for extremely rapid operations. By running the experiment directly on the FPGA, they could quickly generate a "best guess" of how fast the qubit was losing energy using only a few measurements. This eliminated the need for slower data transfers to a conventional computer.

Programming FPGAs for such specialized tasks can be challenging. Even so, the researchers succeeded in updating the controller's internal Bayesian model after every single qubit measurement. That allowed the system to continually refine its understanding of the qubit's condition in real time.

As a result, the controller now keeps pace with the qubit's changing environment. Measurements and adjustments happen on nearly the same timescale as the fluctuations themselves, making the system roughly one hundred times faster than previously demonstrated.

The work also revealed something new. Scientists did not previously know just how quickly fluctuations occur in superconducting qubits. These experiments have now provided that insight.

Commercial Quantum Hardware Meets Advanced Control

FPGAs have long been used in other scientific and engineering fields. In this case, the researchers used a commercially available FPGA based controller from Quantum Machines called the OPX1000. The system can be programmed in a language similar to Python, which many physicists already use, making it more accessible to research groups worldwide.

The integration of this controller with advanced quantum hardware was made possible through close collaboration between the Niels Bohr Institute research group led by Associate Professor Morten Kjaergaard and Chalmers University, where the quantum processing unit was designed and fabricated. "The controller enables very tight integration between logic, measurements and feedforward: these components made our experiment possible," says Morten Kjærgaard.

Why Real Time Calibration Matters for Quantum Computers

Quantum technologies promise powerful new capabilities, though practical large scale quantum computers are still under development. Progress often comes incrementally, but occasionally major steps forward occur.

By uncovering these previously hidden dynamics, the findings reshape how scientists think about testing and calibrating superconducting quantum processors. With current materials and manufacturing methods, moving toward real time monitoring and adjustment appears essential for improving reliability. The results also highlight the importance of partnerships between academic research and industry, along with creative uses of available technology.

"Nowadays, in quantum processing units in general, the overall performance is not determined by the best qubits, but by the worst ones: those are the ones we need to focus on. The surprise from our work is that a 'good' qubit can turn into a 'bad' one in fractions of a second, rather than minutes or hours.

"With our algorithm, the fast control hardware can pinpoint which qubit is 'good' or 'bad' basically in real time. We can also gather useful statistics on the 'bad` qubits in seconds instead of hours or days.

"We still cannot explain a large fraction of the fluctuations we observe. Understanding and controlling the physics behind such fluctuations in qubit properties will be necessary for scaling quantum processors to a useful size," Fabrizio says.

Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10713. Ambulance driver accused of leaving chest pain patient to Uber home after getting lost

A private ambulance driver in Cleveland, Ohio, has been accused of abandoning a patient after getting lost, telling her he was “done driving for the day” before calling an Uber home.

The incident happened on Wednesday, October 28, while the woman was being taken to Cleveland Clinic with chest pain, according to Arizona’s Family.

As the story spread online, the Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975 stepped in to clarify that the driver did not work for Cleveland EMS.

“We want to clarify it was NOT a Cleveland EMS ambulance, but rather a provider working on a private ambulance,” the union wrote. “We stand by our EMTs, Paramedics, and Dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it.”

The union also urged people to “research the facts before blindly sharing AI-generated images and articles,” pointing to an image that had been circulating alongside the story.

The driver worked for Lynx EMS, a private ambulance company. He reportedly got lost on the way to the hospital before allegedly telling the patient he was done for the day and leaving in an Uber.

A Cleveland EMS unit was sent to the scene, where paramedics treated the woman and took her to the hospital.

Lynx said it had taken immediate steps to address the situation and is reviewing the incident, but declined to comment further as it involves personnel and patient matters.

#10712. ChatGPT as a therapist? New study reveals serious ethical risks

As more people seek mental health advice from ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs), new research suggests these AI chatbots may not be ready for that role. The study found that even when instructed to use established psychotherapy approaches, the systems consistently fail to meet professional ethics standards set by organizations such as the American Psychological Association.

Researchers from Brown University, working closely with mental health professionals, identified repeated patterns of problematic behavior. In testing, chatbots mishandled crisis situations, gave responses that reinforced harmful beliefs about users or others, and used language that created the appearance of empathy without genuine understanding.

"In this work, we present a practitioner-informed framework of 15 ethical risks to demonstrate how LLM counselors violate ethical standards in mental health practice by mapping the model's behavior to specific ethical violations," the researchers wrote in their study. "We call on future work to create ethical, educational and legal standards for LLM counselors -- standards that are reflective of the quality and rigor of care required for human-facilitated psychotherapy."

The findings were presented at the AAAI/ACM Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Ethics and Society. The research team is affiliated with Brown's Center for Technological Responsibility, Reimagination and Redesign.

Zainab Iftikhar, a Ph.D. candidate in computer science at Brown who led the study, set out to examine whether carefully worded prompts could guide AI systems to behave more ethically in mental health settings. Prompts are written instructions designed to steer a model's output without retraining it or adding new data.

"Prompts are instructions that are given to the model to guide its behavior for achieving a specific task," Iftikhar said. "You don't change the underlying model or provide new data, but the prompt helps guide the model's output based on its pre-existing knowledge and learned patterns.

"For example, a user might prompt the model with: 'Act as a cognitive behavioral therapist to help me reframe my thoughts,' or 'Use principles of dialectical behavior therapy to assist me in understanding and managing my emotions.' While these models do not actually perform these therapeutic techniques like a human would, they rather use their learned patterns to generate responses that align with the concepts of CBT or DBT based on the input prompt provided."

People regularly share these prompt strategies on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and Reddit. Beyond individual experimentation, many consumer facing mental health chatbots are built by applying therapy related prompts to general purpose LLMs. That makes it especially important to understand whether prompting alone can make AI counseling safer.

Testing AI Chatbots in Simulated Counseling

To evaluate the systems, the researchers observed seven trained peer counselors who had experience with cognitive behavioral therapy. These counselors conducted self counseling sessions with AI models prompted to act as CBT therapists. The models tested included versions of OpenAI's GPT Series, Anthropic's Claude, and Meta's Llama.

The team then selected simulated chats based on real human counseling conversations. Three licensed clinical psychologists reviewed those transcripts to flag possible ethical violations.

The analysis uncovered 15 distinct risks grouped into five broad categories:

The Accountability Gap in AI Mental Health

Iftikhar noted that human therapists can also make mistakes. The key difference is oversight.

"For human therapists, there are governing boards and mechanisms for providers to be held professionally liable for mistreatment and malpractice," Iftikhar said. "But when LLM counselors make these violations, there are no established regulatory frameworks."

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest AI has no place in mental health care. Tools powered by artificial intelligence could help expand access, particularly for people who face high costs or limited availability of licensed professionals. However, the study highlights the need for clear safeguards, responsible deployment, and stronger regulatory structures before relying on these systems in high stakes situations.

For now, Iftikhar hopes the work encourages caution.

"If you're talking to a chatbot about mental health, these are some things that people should be looking out for," she said.

Ellie Pavlick, a Brown computer science professor who was not involved in the research, said the study underscores the importance of carefully examining AI systems used in sensitive areas like mental health. Pavlick leads ARIA, a National Science Foundation AI research institute at Brown focused on building trustworthy AI assistants.

"The reality of AI today is that it's far easier to build and deploy systems than to evaluate and understand them," Pavlick said. "This paper required a team of clinical experts and a study that lasted for more than a year in order to demonstrate these risks. Most work in AI today is evaluated using automatic metrics which, by design, are static and lack a human in the loop."

She added that the study could serve as a model for future research aimed at improving safety in AI mental health tools.

"There is a real opportunity for AI to play a role in combating the mental health crisis that our society is facing, but it's of the utmost importance that we take the time to really critique and evaluate our systems every step of the way to avoid doing more harm than good," Pavlick said. "This work offers a good example of what that can look like."

#10710. Scientists built the hardest AI test ever and the results are surprising

As artificial intelligence systems began scoring extremely high on long used academic benchmarks, researchers noticed a growing issue. The tests that once challenged machines were no longer difficult enough. Well known evaluations such as the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) exam, which had previously been seen as demanding, now fail to properly measure the capabilities of today's advanced AI models.

To solve this problem, a worldwide group of nearly 1,000 researchers, including a professor from Texas A&M University, developed a new type of test. Their goal was to build an exam that is broad, difficult, and grounded in expert human knowledge in ways that current AI systems still struggle to handle.

The result is "Humanity's Last Exam" (HLE), a 2,500 question assessment covering mathematics, humanities, natural sciences, ancient languages, and a wide range of highly specialized academic fields. Details of the project appear in a paper published in Nature, and additional information about the exam is available at lastexam.ai.

Among the many contributors is Dr. Tung Nguyen, instructional associate professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Texas A&M. Nguyen helped write and refine many of the exam questions.

"When AI systems start performing extremely well on human benchmarks, it's tempting to think they're approaching human-level understanding," Nguyen said. "But HLE reminds us that intelligence isn't just about pattern recognition -- it's about depth, context and specialized expertise."

The purpose of the exam was not to trick or defeat human test takers. Instead, the goal was to carefully identify areas where AI systems still fall short.

Specialists from around the world wrote and reviewed the questions included in Humanity's Last Exam. Each problem was carefully designed so it has one clear, verifiable answer. The questions were also crafted to prevent quick solutions through simple internet searches.

The topics come from advanced academic challenges. Some tasks involve translating ancient Palmyrene inscriptions, while others require identifying tiny anatomical structures in birds or analyzing detailed features of Biblical Hebrew pronunciation.

Researchers tested every question against leading AI systems. If any model was able to answer a question correctly, that question was removed from the final exam. This process ensured the test remained just beyond what current AI systems can reliably solve.

Early testing confirmed that the strategy worked. Even powerful AI models struggled with the exam. GPT-4o achieved a score of 2.7 percent, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet reached 4.1 percent. OpenAI's o1 model performed somewhat better with 8 percent. The most capable systems so far, including Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6, have reached accuracy levels between about 40 percent and 50 percent.

Nguyen explained that the issue of AI surpassing older tests is more than a technical concern. He contributed 73 of the 2,500 publicly available questions in HLE, the second highest number among contributors, and wrote the most questions related to mathematics and computer science.

"Without accurate assessment tools, policymakers, developers and users risk misinterpreting what AI systems can actually do," he said. "Benchmarks provide the foundation for measuring progress and identifying risks."

According to the research team, high scores on tests originally designed for humans do not necessarily indicate genuine intelligence. Those benchmarks mainly measure how well AI can complete specific tasks created for human learners, rather than capturing deeper understanding.

Despite the dramatic name, Humanity's Last Exam is not meant to suggest that humans are becoming obsolete. Instead, it highlights the large amount of knowledge and expertise that still remains uniquely human.

"This isn't a race against AI," Nguyen said. "It's a method for understanding where these systems are strong and where they struggle. That understanding helps us build safer, more reliable technologies. And, importantly, it reminds us why human expertise still matters."

Humanity's Last Exam is designed to serve as a durable and transparent benchmark for future AI systems. To support that goal, the researchers have released some questions publicly while keeping the majority hidden so that AI models cannot simply memorize the answers.

"For now, Humanity's Last Exam stands as one of the clearest assessments of the gap between AI and human intelligence," Nguyen said, "and despite rapid technological advances, it remains wide."

Nguyen emphasized that the scale of the project demonstrates the value of collaboration across disciplines and countries.

"What made this project extraordinary was the scale," he said. "Experts from nearly every discipline contributed. It wasn't just computer scientists; it was historians, physicists, linguists, medical researchers. That diversity is exactly what exposes the gaps in today's AI systems -- perhaps ironically, it's humans working together."

Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

At the lowest level of abstraction, researchers search manually and cross-reference by hand.

#10706. Scientists discover AI can make humans more creative

Artificial intelligence (AI) is commonly viewed as a technology designed to automate work and potentially replace human labor. However, new research from Swansea University offers a different perspective. The findings suggest that AI can also function as a creative collaborator that encourages exploration, engagement, and inspiration.

Researchers from the University's Computer Science Department carried out one of the largest studies so far examining how people work alongside AI during creative design tasks. More than 800 participants joined an online experiment where they used an AI-supported system to design virtual cars.

Rather than quietly optimizing designs behind the scenes, the system used a method called MAP-Elites to produce visual galleries filled with many different design possibilities. These galleries showed a wide spectrum of car concepts, including highly effective designs, unusual ideas, and even some intentionally flawed options.

Turing Fellow Dr. Sean Walton, Associate Professor of Computer Science and the study's lead author, explained: "People often think of AI as something that speeds up tasks or improves efficiency, but our findings suggest something far more interesting. When people were shown AI-generated design suggestions, they spent more time on the task, produced better designs and felt more involved. It was not just about efficiency. It was about creativity and collaboration."

Why Traditional AI Evaluation May Be Too Limited

The study, published in the ACM journal Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems, also highlights a problem with how AI design tools are typically assessed. Standard metrics often focus on simple behaviors, such as how frequently users click on or copy AI suggestions. According to the researchers, these measures overlook important aspects of the experience, including how the technology influences people's thoughts, emotions, and willingness to explore new ideas.

The Swansea researchers argue that AI systems should be evaluated using broader methods that capture these deeper effects. Understanding how AI shapes human thinking and engagement could provide a more complete picture of its impact.

Dr. Walton emphasized that variety in AI-generated output played a crucial role in the experiment. "Our study highlights the importance of diversity in AI output. Participants responded most positively to galleries that included a wide variety of ideas, including bad ones! These helped them move beyond their initial assumptions and explore a broader design space. This structured diversity prevented early fixation and encouraged creative risk-taking.

"As AI becomes increasingly embedded in creative fields, from engineering and architecture to music and game design, understanding how humans and intelligent systems work together is essential. As the technology evolves, the question is not only what AI can do but how it can help us think, create and collaborate more effectively."

Materials provided by Swansea University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10702. AI-powered robot learns how to harvest tomatoes more efficiently

Farm labor shortages are pushing agriculture toward greater automation, especially when it comes to harvesting. But not all crops are easy for machines to handle. Tomatoes, for example, grow in clusters, which means a robot must carefully select ripe fruit while leaving unripe ones untouched. This requires precise control and smart decision-making.

To tackle this challenge, Assistant Professor Takuya Fujinaga of Osaka Metropolitan University's Graduate School of Engineering developed a system that trains robots to assess how easy each tomato is to harvest before attempting to pick it.

His approach combines image recognition with statistical analysis to determine the best angle for picking each fruit. The robot analyzes visual details such as the tomato itself, its stems, and whether it is hidden behind leaves or other parts of the plant. These inputs guide the robot in choosing the most effective way to approach and pick the fruit.

From Detection to "Harvest-Ease" Decision-Making

This method shifts away from traditional systems that focus only on detecting and identifying fruit. Instead, Fujinaga introduces what he calls "harvest-ease estimation." "This moves beyond simply asking 'can a robot pick a tomato?' to thinking about 'how likely is a successful pick?', which is more meaningful for real-world farming," he explained.

In testing, the system achieved an 81% success rate, exceeding expectations. About one-quarter of the successful picks came from tomatoes that were harvested from the side after an initial front-facing attempt failed. This indicates the robot can adjust its approach when the first attempt is not successful.

The research underscores how many variables affect robotic harvesting, including how tomatoes cluster, the shape and position of stems, surrounding leaves, and visual obstruction. "This research establishes 'ease of harvesting' as a quantitatively evaluable metric, bringing us one step closer to the realization of agricultural robots that can make informed decisions and act intelligently," Fujinaga said.

Future of Human-Robot Collaboration in Farming

Looking ahead, Fujinaga envisions robots that can independently judge when crops are ready to be picked. "This is expected to usher in a new form of agriculture where robots and humans collaborate," he explained. "Robots will automatically harvest tomatoes that are easy to pick, while humans will handle the more challenging fruits."

The findings were published in Smart Agricultural Technology.

#10700. Modern HTML Forms: Building Accessible, Secure, and User-Friendly Experiences

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Forms are among the most important components of modern websites. They allow users to register accounts, submit contact requests, search for information, complete purchases, and interact with web applications.

Despite their apparent simplicity, forms can introduce significant usability and development challenges. Poorly labeled fields, unclear validation messages, inaccessible controls, and unreliable submission behavior can prevent users from completing even basic tasks.

Modern HTML provides many built-in features that help developers create more reliable forms with less JavaScript. When combined with semantic markup, thoughtful CSS, and carefully designed validation, these features can improve both usability and maintainability.

This article explores practical techniques for building modern web forms that are accessible, responsive, and easier to maintain.

A well-structured form begins with the correct HTML elements. Native controls provide built-in browser behavior and communicate their purpose to assistive technologies.

Each control has an explicitly associated label. The name attributes identify the fields when form data is submitted, while autocomplete helps browsers recognize common information types.

The required attribute indicates that a field must be completed before a normal browser submission can proceed.

These native features reduce the need for custom code and provide a more consistent starting point across browsers.

HTML provides several input types designed for specific kinds of information.

For example, type="email" enables browser validation for email-shaped input, while type="tel" identifies a telephone number field and can prompt mobile browsers to display a suitable keyboard.

Selecting appropriate input types improves the user experience, especially on mobile devices.

However, native validation has limits. An email input does not establish that an address exists or belongs to the person entering it. Similarly, a URL input does not guarantee that a submitted address is safe to access.

Client-side validation should therefore be treated as a usability feature, not as a substitute for server-side validation.

Browser controls can look different across platforms. A small set of reusable CSS rules can make a form feel more consistent while preserving native functionality.

The box-sizing: border-box declaration makes width calculations more predictable because padding and borders are included in the declared width.

Using font: inherit helps form controls remain consistent with the surrounding typography.

The visible focus outline is equally important. Keyboard users need to identify which control currently receives focus, so removing browser outlines without an accessible replacement should be avoided.

HTML can handle many common validation requirements without a custom script.

For example, a username field can use length constraints:

A numeric field can define a suitable range:

These attributes help the browser identify certain invalid values before submission.

Developers should choose constraints based on actual application requirements. For example, a quantity field may require a positive integer, while a measurement field might legitimately accept decimals.

Custom JavaScript validation is useful when rules depend on other fields, remote data, or business logic. For basic requirements, native HTML validation is often simpler and easier to maintain.

A useful validation message explains what went wrong and how the user can correct it.

For more complex forms, developers may need to provide custom feedback:

JavaScript can use the browser's constraint validation API to identify invalid input:

This example prevents submission when the email field is invalid and displays a more specific message.

For production forms, validation should be coordinated across all relevant fields. Errors should remain associated with their controls, be communicated accessibly, and not rely on color alone.

The server must repeat relevant validation because client-side checks can be bypassed.

Users may accidentally submit a form multiple times by clicking a button repeatedly or interacting with a slow interface.

For an asynchronous form, the submit button can be disabled while a request is in progress.

This is an illustrative example and assumes that the form has an appropriate action URL and that the server accepts the submitted fields.

A real application should provide accessible inline status messages instead of relying on alert(). It should also consider authentication, server-side error responses, network timeouts, and whether retrying a request could create duplicate records.

For operations that must not be repeated, server-side idempotency controls may be necessary. Disabling a button alone cannot guarantee that a request is processed only once.

Forms frequently collect personal or business information, so security must be part of their design.

Validate all submitted data on the server.

Apply appropriate authorization checks to sensitive operations.

Use CSRF protection where required by the application's authentication architecture.

Escape or safely render user-provided content to reduce injection risks.

Avoid placing passwords, tokens, or sensitive personal information in URLs.

Apply appropriate rate limits to public-facing endpoints.

HTML validation helps users correct mistakes, but it does not establish trust in submitted data.

For example, a hidden input containing a user's role must never be treated as authoritative proof of that role. A malicious client can change the value before submission.

Security decisions belong on the server, where the application can verify permissions and enforce its rules.

Forms should remain usable on mobile devices without forcing users to zoom, scroll horizontally, or interact with cramped controls.

A responsive form container can use flexible sizing:

The min() function limits the container width while allowing it to adapt to smaller viewports. Logical properties such as margin-inline also make the layout more adaptable to different writing directions.

Developers should test forms at narrow widths and with browser zoom enabled. Long labels, validation messages, and translated content should be allowed to wrap naturally.

It is also worth checking that touch targets are comfortable to use and that the form does not depend on hover effects to communicate important information.

A form that works when every field contains valid data may still fail under realistic conditions.

Submitting the form with required fields empty.

Navigating every control using a keyboard.

Checking focus indicators and error announcements.

Testing on mobile-sized screens and at increased zoom.

Simulating server errors and network interruptions.

Verifying that the server rejects invalid or unauthorized requests.

Confirming that successful submissions provide clear feedback.

Automated browser tests can cover common validation and submission scenarios. Manual testing remains valuable for checking whether error messages are understandable and whether the form feels usable to people with different accessibility needs.

The most reliable forms are designed to handle failure clearly, not just to demonstrate a successful submission.

Modern HTML provides a strong foundation for building accessible and maintainable forms. Semantic elements, appropriate input types, native validation, and reusable CSS can reduce unnecessary JavaScript while improving the user experience.

When custom validation or asynchronous submission is required, developers should add it carefully and preserve clear feedback, keyboard support, and server-side security controls.

A well-designed form does more than collect information. It guides users through a task, helps them recover from mistakes, and communicates what happens next. By treating usability, accessibility, and security as connected parts of the same design process, developers can build forms that are more reliable and easier to maintain.

#10698. DNA robots could deliver drugs and hunt viruses inside your body

Imagine tiny robots made from DNA moving through the bloodstream, delivering drugs exactly where they are needed and targeting threats such as cancer cells or viruses. These microscopic machines could also assemble ultra-precise data storage systems and computing devices at the nanometer scale. Although the possibilities are remarkable, most DNA robots today remain in early experimental stages and are better understood as proof of concept rather than practical tools.

Researchers are exploring how DNA can be engineered into working machines using creative design approaches. These include building rigid DNA joints, incorporating flexible components, and using folding techniques inspired by origami. By applying principles from larger-scale robotics such as rigid, compliant and origami robots, scientists are adapting familiar mechanical concepts to the nanoscale. This allows DNA-based systems to carry out controlled and repeatable tasks despite their extremely small size.

Guiding the motion of DNA robots in a constantly shifting molecular environment is a major challenge. To address this, scientists have developed control systems that help these machines behave in predictable ways. One important method involves DNA strand displacement, a biochemical process that enables precise programming of movement using specific DNA sequences labeled as "fuel" and "structure."

In addition to biochemical control, external physical signals such as electric fields, magnetic fields, and light can direct how these robots move. Together, these approaches provide a toolkit for fine-tuning the behavior of DNA machines with a high degree of accuracy.

The potential uses for DNA robots extend well beyond laboratory experiments. In medicine, they could function as "nano-surgeons," locating diseased cells and delivering targeted treatments with precision. Researchers are also exploring whether these machines could capture viruses like SARS-CoV-2, with future systems potentially operating as fully autonomous drug delivery platforms.

DNA robots may also play a role in advanced manufacturing. Acting as programmable templates, they could position nanoparticles with sub-nanometer accuracy. This capability could lead to breakthroughs in molecular computing and highly efficient optical devices that outperform current technologies.

Despite rapid progress, several obstacles remain. Moving from large-scale systems to molecular machines introduces challenges such as Brownian motion, which makes precise control more difficult. Many current DNA robot designs are still relatively simple and operate in isolation, limiting their usefulness in complex real-world environments.

There are also gaps in foundational knowledge. Researchers still lack detailed databases describing the mechanical properties of DNA structures, and simulation tools for predicting behavior at this scale are not yet fully developed.

To overcome these barriers, scientists emphasize the need for collaboration across disciplines. Proposed solutions include creating standardized DNA "parts libraries," using artificial intelligence to improve design and simulation, and advancing bio-manufacturing methods. Progress in these areas will be essential for scaling DNA robots and integrating them into practical applications in healthcare, manufacturing, and beyond.

"The robots of tomorrow won't just be made of metal and plastic," says the research team. "They will be biological, programmable, and intelligent. They will be the tools that allow us to finally master the molecular world."

#10697. Niftski breaks Super Mario Bros. world record in Mario costume as perfect run comes within 2 frames

Super Mario Bros. speedrunner Niftski set a new any% world record on Halloween while dressed as Mario, completing the NES classic in 4:54.299 and moving within two frames of a theoretically perfect run.

The performance lowered Niftski’s previous record of 4:54.332, set in August 2026, by 33 milliseconds. It also pushed the game’s human leaderboard closer than ever to the current benchmark for perfection.

Niftski has spent years pushing Super Mario Bros. toward its limits. In 2021, he became the first player to complete the game in under 4:55, a milestone that was compared to breaking the four-minute mile in speedrunning.

The record chase has since become a battle between Niftski and Brazilian runner LeKukie. LeKukie briefly claimed the world record in June with a 4:54.365 run, cutting the gap to the theoretical limit to six frames before Niftski reclaimed the top spot two months later.

“Only 2 frames (33 milliseconds) stand between this run and absolute perfection / TAS tie,” Niftski wrote after the run.

4:54.299 SMB1 ANY% WORLD RECORD ON HALLOWEEN WHILE LARPING AS MARIO! It doesn't even feel real that I actually achieved this, but here we are. Only 2 frames (33 milliseconds) stand between this run and absolute perfection / TAS tie. 4:54.265 next! pic.twitter.com/S1ZpmEMG4c

That target is based on a tool-assisted speedrun, or TAS, which uses frame-by-frame inputs to determine how quickly the game can theoretically be completed. The relevant benchmark is 4:54.265, created under the same rules used for real-time runs.

There is an even faster TAS time of 4:54.032, but that version uses simultaneous left-and-right inputs that are impossible on a standard NES controller and are banned from human attempts. The 4:54.265 benchmark is therefore treated as the practical theoretical limit for the category.

Super Mario Bros. runs at 60 frames per second, meaning each frame lasts roughly 16.7 milliseconds. The game also uses 21-frame cycles to determine when most levels are completed. That means a runner can lose a few frames in some stages without losing time on the final clock, as long as they still reach the next cycle.

Mario speedrunner claims he’s being derailed on way to ‘perfect’ run

Speedrunner breaks Super Mario Bros world record by the thinnest of margins

Minecraft speedrunner finally sets world record one year after devastating last-second fail

The final level, World 8-4, works differently. It does not offer the same frame-rule cushion, so every successful jump, movement and button press can affect the final result. That is where the remaining gap between Niftski’s record and the TAS benchmark must be erased.

LeKukie remains close behind in the race, and both runners have been streaming attempts at the same impossible-looking goal.

Niftski’s latest record proves that the barrier is no longer theoretical in the way it once seemed. The game has been played for more than 40 years, yet the fastest human performance is now separated from machine-perfect play by less than the blink of an eye.

In 2021, breaking 4:55 felt like the end of what a person could do in Super Mario Bros. Now the question is whether Niftski, LeKukie or another runner can string together the final two frames and complete the first human TAS tie.
